title: Wealth, inheritance, housing, debt, and tax measurement require harmonized evidence before mobility and power can be compared across countries
source_unit: Longmuir et al., Scientific Data 2026, Wealth Composition, Distribution, and Transmission: The Graduate Center Wealth Project Data Warehouse
geography: Multiple countries and time periods; international wealth, household-balance-sheet, inequality, and wealth-transfer-tax evidence

observations.period: 2026 data warehouse release; multiple countries and time periods

denominator.unit: open data warehouse integrating cross-country wealth evidence

database_components.value: The warehouse combines Wealth Topography, Wealth Inequality Trends, and Estate, Inheritance and Gift Taxes databases

wealth_composition.value: The framework separates financial wealth, housing wealth, business wealth, other assets, and debt in household balance sheets

transmission.value: The resource links private wealth distribution to intergenerational transmission and wealth-transfer taxation

interpretation.value: Ownership and mobility cannot be understood from income alone; asset composition, liabilities, inheritance, and tax rules shape the reproduction of advantage

observations.method: The data descriptor harmonizes existing wealth, balance-sheet, distributional, tax, and legal-policy sources and attaches metadata describing methods and source provenance.
observations.uncertainty: This is a data resource and methodology paper, not a single new causal estimate. Underlying sources differ in coverage, definitions, valuation, population, and survey or administrative design.
observations.subgroup: Countries, years, wealth percentiles, households or individuals, asset classes, debt holders, heirs, and taxpayers across different legal regimes.
observations.counterinterpretation: More harmonized data can expose uncertainty rather than eliminate it; wealth concepts that include or exclude pensions, human capital, informal assets, or public benefits can produce materially different mobility conclusions.

denominator.unit: countries covered by systematic comparison of estate, inheritance, and gift taxation

tax_comparison.value: The project enables systematic comparison of wealth-transfer taxation across more than 160 countries

policy_features.value: The tax database includes revenues, rates, exemption thresholds, tax schedules, and introduction or repeal dates

historical_depth.value: Some wealth-transfer-tax information extends back to the eighteenth century

interpretation.value: Intergenerational mobility is partly institutionalized through tax design, not only determined by family assets or individual effort

observations.method: Researchers extract and harmonize tax features from legal documents, administrative and research sources, and historical policy records, with source and methodological metadata.
observations.uncertainty: Tax-law presence, rates, and exemptions do not directly reveal effective incidence, compliance, avoidance, valuation, or actual transfers. Historical legal records may be uneven across countries and periods.
observations.subgroup: Heirs, donors, estates, asset classes, family structures, tax jurisdictions, and households with different access to legal and financial planning.
observations.counterinterpretation: A formal inheritance tax can coexist with low revenue or limited redistribution; low taxation can reflect broad exemptions, administrative constraints, or other public systems rather than a simple policy preference.

denominator.unit: warehouse of country-year-percentile wealth-distribution observations assembled from heterogeneous sources

distribution_statistics.value: The warehouse includes Gini indices, wealth shares held by distributional groups, and average net wealth along the distribution

source_heterogeneity.value: The underlying evidence includes academic studies, government and corporate research, cross-national datasets, and official statistics

metadata.value: Rows include geography, year, percentile, source, variable codes, long descriptions, and methodological metadata

interpretation.value: Comparative wealth claims should be treated as source-conditional estimates with visible provenance, not as one frictionless global ranking

observations.method: The project stores harmonized long-format observations and metadata, draws on multiple source datasets, and documents conceptual grids, conversions, and reproducibility code.
observations.uncertainty: Harmonization cannot fully remove differences in survey frames, wealth definitions, valuation dates, top-tail coverage, debt treatment, or missing data. The authors note that estimates can be heterogeneous and contested.
observations.subgroup: Wealth percentiles, country-years, source families, asset categories, and populations measured by household or individual units.
observations.counterinterpretation: A single standardized statistic can be useful for monitoring if its construction is transparent; multiple estimates may reflect genuine alternative concepts rather than mere noise.

observations.period: 2026 release; research access and reproduction boundary

denominator.unit: open data descriptor and downloadable warehouse resource

open_access.value: The warehouse is released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license through a public repository

microdata_boundary.value: The project provides aggregated secondary data from legally obtained sources and cannot provide some underlying HFCS and Luxembourg Wealth Study microdata

reproducibility.value: Replication code, source tables, conversion tables, and metadata are provided to reconstruct or audit the harmonized warehouse

interpretation.value: Public trend mining benefits from separating reusable aggregate evidence from inaccessible respondent-level microdata and documenting where each inference stops

observations.method: The paper documents data files, source tables, code, metadata, legal access conditions, and limitations on underlying microdata availability.
observations.uncertainty: Reproduction depends on access to original source data, legal permissions, changing source vintages, and the authors' classification and conversion choices; open access to the warehouse does not mean all underlying inputs are open.
observations.subgroup: Researchers, policymakers, data users, and populations represented in aggregated wealth and tax indicators rather than directly observed in this atlas.
observations.counterinterpretation: A strong documentation layer improves auditability but cannot make aggregate wealth statistics equivalent to respondent-level lived experience or guarantee that every original estimate is comparable.

related_sources.claim: Canonical open-access Scientific Data article describing the Graduate Center Wealth Project data warehouse.
Public repository for the warehouse files and supplementary source tables.

boundary: This record adds a measurement and policy-infrastructure layer for wealth composition, distribution, inheritance, and tax transmission. It does not ingest respondent-level microdata, estimate causal mobility effects, provide a single global wealth truth, or make every underlying source comparable; it is a documented aggregate data warehouse and data descriptor.
